what_it_does: After a chip's logic blocks are placed on a floorplan, the wires connecting them must be routed — a step called detailed routing. When the initial routing has too many design-rule violations (wires crossing, spacing rules broken), the standard fix is to rip out some wires in a rectangular window of the layout and re-route them from scratch; this is called rip-up and reroute. The problem is choosing which window to work on next: picking windows at random or in a fixed scan order wastes time on areas with few problems while neglecting congested hotspots. This paper trains a reinforcement-learning agent — an algorithm that learns good decisions by trial and reward, similar to how a game-playing AI learns chess moves — to pick the size and position of the next rip-up window based on where violations are currently clustered. Over many training iterations the agent learns to target the most congested regions first, finishing routing with fewer total violations in competitive time.
